title: Master Class | 700 Elo | Chess Speedrun | Grandmaster Naroditsky

moves.spoken: c6 is a poor move on two counts: it robs the knight of its natural c6 square and it fails to defend the e-pawn.
moves.teaches: A pawn move that both blocks your own knight's square and leaves a pawn hanging is doubly bad.

moves.spoken: So we simply take on e5, and if Black wants the pawn back he'll have to spend time and moves for it.

Qa5-check regains the pawn but drags the queen out while nothing develops. Block with Nc3, not the tempting Bd2 — Bd2 only shoves the queen toward the pawn it was going to take anyway, and it's an awful square for the bishop.
moves.teaches: Meet a check with a developing move, not one that improves the opponent's plan while misplacing your piece.

moves.spoken: Nf3 develops and defends e4; now two pieces are out, the queen is harassed, and Black's knight is stuck with both of its squares blocked by pawns.
moves.teaches: When the opponent burns time on the queen, pile up developed pieces and the edge snowballs.

moves.spoken: Ng5 manufactures our own fried liver — it hits the queen and sets up Bc4 against f7. Moving a piece twice is usually wrong, but a lead in development buys you that liberty.
moves.teaches: A big development lead licenses breaking the rules — even moving one piece twice for a concrete attack.

moves.spoken: Bc4 trains onto f7 — but be careful: b5 is coming, and a move isn't good just because it makes a threat.
moves.teaches: Don't equate a threatening move with a good move; check the opponent's reply first.

moves.spoken: A calculation lesson: Nxf7 forks queen and rook, but grabbing the rook lets Black trap the knight. When a line fails, don't restart from the top — back up to the last move where you had a choice. Taking the rook wasn't forced; Bb3 first keeps the knight defended, then collect the rook. Uncouple your emotions from the calculation.
moves.teaches: When a variation fails, backtrack to the last branching point, not the first move — and judge it analytically, not by taste.

moves.spoken: And note Bxf7 is also simply crushing — there was more than one road in.

Up a queen, resist grabbing every scrap — but do take what's literally free. Qh5-check, then a knight sacrifice on g6 rips it open, Qa5-check swings across, and a picture mate follows because the bishop already covers d6.
moves.teaches: With a decisive material lead, take what's free and steer for the clean mate, not extra material.

moves.spoken: Black's best defense was d5 — it opens the bishop and hits ours, and we can't take because of the pin. But don't be intimidated: after we castle, that d5-pawn becomes a blessing, since exd5 can rip open the e-file against the stranded king.
moves.teaches: A pawn that pins your bishop now can become a target the moment you castle and can capture it.
